Coordinate multiple agents

Fan-out over the ready queue, planner/executor splits via plan composition, shared-lab investigation, what happens when a claim holder dies, and the git hooks that check a repo lock.

On this page

  • What the loser of a race sees
  • Planner and executor, split by plan composition
  • Shared-lab investigation

Coordinating multiple coding agents with Seamless means pointing N workers - Claude Code, Codex, or any MCP client - at one shared, dependency-aware task queue with atomic lease-based claiming: every worker runs the same claim loop, exactly one wins each task, and a dead worker's lease expires instead of stranding its work. There is no scheduler process and no orchestrator - the coordination is the workers cooperating over the queue.

One agent with memory is a better agent. Several agents with shared memory and no coordination is a worse outcome than one - they duplicate work, contradict each other's writes, and discover the same dead end in parallel.

This page is the part of Seamless that exists for the fleet: how N agents divide work without colliding, and what happens when one of them dies holding something.

Fan-out over the ready queue

The pattern is a seeder and N identical workers. The seeder decomposes the work once:

tasks_add title="extract the parser"          → 01K...A
tasks_add title="port callers"  depends_on=A  → 01K...B
tasks_add title="delete the old path" depends_on=B

depends_on is the whole schedule. A task is ready when no blocker is still open or in_progress; either done or dropped unblocks a dependent, because work abandoned on purpose should not wedge the queue forever. Cycles are rejected at creation rather than discovered at scheduling time.

A schedule is corrected in place. When a blocker turns out to be the wrong task, tasks_update remove_depends_on=<wrong> drops it and add_depends_on=<right> adds the right one (seam task unblock and seam task block from a shell), so the task keeps its id and nothing that cites it goes stale. Removing a task's last unfinished blocker makes it ready; naming an id that is not a blocker changes nothing and the answer says so.

Every worker then runs the same loop, and needs no knowledge of the others:

tasks_claim fails with no active session to claim as if the connection has no session. That is not incidental strictness: the claim records who holds the task, and a claim by nobody could never be released, reclaimed, or attributed. A Claude Code or Codex worker needs no setup for this: its tool calls are bound to its own session, so its claims name it even with several workers in one repo.

What the loser of a race sees

tasks_ready orders oldest-created first, ties broken by id. That order is stable and identical for every worker - which means every worker tries the same task first. Contention on the head of the queue is the designed behavior, not a thundering-herd bug, because losing is cheap and unambiguous:

task already claimed: task "01K7ABCD..." held by "01K7SESS..."

The holder is named as a session id, not an agent name. One claim landed; the loser got a clean error, not a corrupted second claim.

What the loser does next matters more than the error. Do not retry the same id - someone is working it, and a retry loop is just a slower way to do nothing. Do not walk to the next id in the list you already have either: that list was read before the race and is now stale in exactly the way that caused the collision. Call tasks_ready again and claim from the fresh list. Two workers that both do this converge on disjoint tasks within one round trip.

Claiming is a coordination signal, not a lock on the files. Nothing physically stops an agent from editing code for a task it did not claim. The model works because well-behaved agents do not collide - not because misbehaving ones cannot.

Planner and executor, split by plan composition

Fan-out works when the work is a flat list. Real work has a design, and a design that lives only in the planner's context dies when that agent does.

A plan is not a primitive - it is everything keyed by plan:<slug>. That is what makes the split possible:

The planner writes With
The narrative - the design and why it looks like that notes_create plan=<slug>
Supporting context - the research behind it More notes, same plan=<slug>
The steps, with their dependencies tasks_add plan=<slug> depends_on=...

The executors never need the planner. They read the narrative note, then work the plan's queue:

tasks_ready plan=<slug>   ─▶ that plan's claimable steps
tasks_claim <id>          ─▶ same race, same rules

Plan steps are excluded from the default queue. tasks_ready and tasks_list skip them unless you pass plan=, so a twelve-step plan does not bury the handful of tasks that are genuinely loose work. This is why a planner can decompose aggressively without drowning every other agent on the machine.

The briefing surfaces each active plan as one rolled-up row rather than a step list:

Plans:
- marketing -- 2/3 done, 1 claimable, 0 in flight
(steps: tasks_ready plan=<slug>; claim: tasks_claim id=<task id>; attach work via the plan:<slug> tag)

That is enough for an arriving agent to decide whether to pick something up, without spending briefing budget on steps it will not touch.

Claude Code's plan mode builds this composition automatically - plan-file saves become notes, approval creates the tracking task. See Tasks & plans.

Shared-lab investigation

Some work does not decompose into tasks at all. Chasing an intermittent bug is N agents trying things, and the expensive failure is two of them trying the same thing an hour apart.

A lab is the shared record for one line of investigation:

lab_open lab=dfu-timeout        ─▶ binds the lab; returns up to 10 recent trials
trial_record title="..." changes="..." expected="..." actual="..." outcome=fail
              metrics={"hz":497}
trial_query outcome=fail metrics_filter={"hz":497}

lab_open binds the lab to the connection the way session_start binds the project, so trial_record inherits it. The context it returns on open is the point: an agent joining an investigation already in progress sees what has been tried before it tries anything.

Record failures, and record them with the expected and actual fields populated. A trial that says what you thought would happen and what did is the only kind another agent can reason from. metrics is an exact-match structured filter, so "every trial where the rate was 497" is a query rather than a reading exercise.

When the investigation resolves, distill it into a memory - a gotcha for the trap, a refuted for the theory that looked right and wasn't. The lab is the working record; it is not the conclusion, and nothing reads it into a briefing.

Leases, crashes, and reclaiming

A claim stamps a lease - 900 seconds by default, overridable with lease_seconds. Four rules cover the model:

  1. Claiming is atomic. A compare-and-set: the write lands only if the task is claimable. The loser gets an error, never a second claim.
  2. Re-claiming refreshes the lease. That is the heartbeat. An agent still working long work keeps its claim by claiming again - there is no separate heartbeat tool, and seam task heartbeat is this path under a clearer name.
  3. An expired lease is reclaimable. Expiry is enforced lazily, inside the claim - there is no background sweeper watching leases.
  4. Closing frees it. tasks_release, tasks_update to done/dropped, or session_end, which releases every claim the session still holds.

Rule 3 has a consequence worth stating plainly, because "reclaimable" is easy to over-read: an expired lease does not put the task back in tasks_ready. The task is still in_progress, and tasks_ready returns only open tasks. Nothing re-queues it, because nothing is scanning for it.

So when an agent dies holding a task, two different clocks are running:

Clock Length What it changes
The lease lease_seconds, default 900s, at most 14400s The task becomes stealable by id - a worker that knows the id can tasks_claim it and win. It is still not in the ready queue
The session idle reap gardener.session_idle_minutes (45) after the last lease lapses, on the gardener's tick The reaper expires the dead session and releases its claims - status back to open, and the task is genuinely back in the queue. A live claim keeps its session live, so the reap never comes while a lease runs

The reaper is the backstop that makes crashes self-healing, and it is the only one that re-queues. A clean session_end does the same thing immediately, which is the real reason a fleet worker should always end its session rather than just exiting.

The reaper runs on the gardener's schedule, once every gardener.interval_minutes, whether or not gardener.enabled is on: that key turns off the gardener's suggestions, never the reaping. See Troubleshooting.

Nobody wants to wait 45 minutes for an obvious corpse, so there is an owner override - the console's Release claim button, or seam task release --force <id>. It force-releases any holder's claim regardless of the lease, and it is deliberately not on the MCP surface: agents get the cooperative protocol, you get the override.

Commit-time lock checks

A repo lock tells cooperating agents that a repository's main branch, or its release tags, are being landed. Two git hooks make git itself check the lock where a guarded ref moves:

  • reference-transaction runs for every ref update in the checkout: a commit, a cherry-pick, git merge --ff-only, a rebase, a reset, a tag, and git update-ref.
  • pre-push runs for the refs a push updates on the remote.

Both run seam lock check. It reads the updates git hands the hook and refuses one that moves a ref one of the repository's locks guards, unless the caller may move it:

Caller Lock held by the caller Held by another session Free
An agent session moves the ref refused refused: take the lock first
An agent with no live session - refused refused: resume or start a session, then take the lock
Anyone else, such as the owner at a terminal - refused moves the ref

An agent session is one the daemon can name. seam sends the agent process that ran git, as every seam call does (process binding), and the daemon answers whether that process belongs to a live session and whether that session holds the lock. An agent may run git through a program of its own, such as a landing script under node or a make target. That program is then the nearest process above git, and no session belongs to it, so seam lock check asks again as each process further up and uses the first answer that names a session.

A caller the daemon binds to no session all the way up is still an agent when its environment says so. Claude Code and Codex mark every command their shell tool runs, and git hands a hook that environment unchanged. Claude Code sets CLAUDECODE=1; it also names its own process in CLAUDE_PID, and when that variable is set the process must be above git, so a marker that outlived its agent (a tmux server an agent started passes its environment to every later pane) does not count. Codex sets CODEX_THREAD_ID, and CODEX_SANDBOX in a sandboxed command. Such an agent has no session to hold the lock with: its session ended (session_end), or no session-start hook ever stamped it. The refusal says to resume the session, with session_start and the name=cc/... or cx/... its briefing printed, or to start one, and then to take the lock. A caller with no marker is treated as anyone else. The markers are a convention between cooperating agents, not a security boundary: an agent can unset them.

The lock is found the way seam lock finds it: by the checkout's origin first, then its host and path. A second clone of the repository, on another machine, is checked against the same lock. A push is checked against the lock of the checkout it is pushed from, whatever URL it goes to.

The hooks need git 2.28 or later, seam on the PATH git runs them with, and repo locks turned on in the server.

Add the hooks to a repository

The reference-transaction hook (the Seamless repository commits this one as .githooks/reference-transaction):

#!/bin/sh

[ "$1" = prepared ] || exit 0

updates=$(cat)
case $updates in
*" refs/"*) ;;
*) exit 0 ;;
esac

if ! command -v seam >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "reference-transaction: seam is not on PATH, so the repository's locks were not checked" >&2
	exit 0
fi
if ! seam lock check --help >/dev/null 2>&1; then
	echo "reference-transaction: this seam has no lock check (it predates repo locks), so the repository's locks were not checked" >&2
	exit 0
fi

printf '%s\n' "$updates" | seam lock check --hook reference-transaction -- "$@"
status=$?
case $status in
0) exit 0 ;;
77) exit 1 ;;
esac
echo "reference-transaction: seam lock check exited $status, so the repository's locks were not checked" >&2
exit 0

The pre-push hook is the same script without the first line (git passes it no state), with --hook pre-push and its own name in the messages. Make both executable, then either:

  • commit them under .githooks/ and run git config core.hooksPath .githooks once per clone. git reads a relative path against each worktree's root, so every worktree runs its own checkout's copy; or
  • copy them into .git/hooks/, which every worktree of the repository shares and which is never committed.

In the Seamless repository, make install-git-hooks sets core.hooksPath to .githooks, which also runs the pre-commit check.

The script refuses only when seam lock check exits 77. Every other outcome lets the update through, so a broken check never wedges git:

  • with no seam on the PATH, or a seam that predates lock check, the hook prints a warning;
  • with the daemon down, or silent for 10 seconds, seam lock check prints a warning and exits 0;
  • with repo locks turned off in the server, or no lock declared for the repository, it exits 0 and prints nothing.

What a refusal means

error: refused: this update moves refs/heads/main, which LOCK example-app main guards, and session cc/1a2b3c holds the lock (since 2026-11-15T18:00:00Z, until 2026-11-15T18:15:00Z).
       Wait for its release, or queue for the lock: seam lock acquire --wait
       --no-verify does not skip the reference-transaction hook, which runs this check on every ref update. The owner's override is a force-release: seam lock release --force, or the console's Locks page.
fatal: in 'prepared' phase, update aborted by the reference-transaction hook
  • Held by another session. Wait for its release, or queue behind the holder with seam lock acquire --wait. The holder is named only where you may see that session; otherwise the line says "another session".
  • Free, and this session does not hold it. An agent session lands only while it holds the lock: run seam lock acquire, then land.
  • A lapsed hold. The holder's lease ran out, so the lock is free again: acquire it before you land.
  • A refused push prints the same, then error: failed to push some refs.
  • After a refused git merge --ff-only, or the merge step of git pull, git has already updated the index and the working tree but leaves the branch where it was. git reset --merge puts the files back.

--no-verify does not skip reference-transaction. The owner's override is a force-release, on the console's Locks page or with seam lock release --force. Like the lock itself, the hooks keep cooperating agents in step; they are not access control.

What is never checked

  • A ref outside refs/: HEAD, ORIG_HEAD, AUTO_MERGE, FETCH_HEAD and a worktree's own HEAD. A commit on a detached HEAD in your own worktree never calls seam lock check, let alone the daemon.
  • git's own namespaces: refs/remotes/, refs/bisect/, refs/rewritten/, refs/worktree/, refs/prefetch/ and refs/stash. A lock may name a ref there, but no hook checks it.
  • An update that leaves a ref where it is.
  • What a fetch brings: its remote-tracking refs and its tags, which the remote already has. A fetch that moves a local branch with an explicit refspec (git fetch origin main:main) is checked. seam lock check reads which git command ran the hook from the process table on macOS and Linux; elsewhere, a transaction that updates a remote-tracking ref is taken for a fetch.
  • clone, pack-refs, gc and maintenance: they bring refs here or rewrite how refs are stored, without moving one.
  • A declaration still waiting for the owner's approval.
  • The other states of a transaction. git runs reference-transaction as a transaction is preparing, once it is prepared, and once it is committed or aborted. Only the prepared state checks.

Hooks off

seam doctor adds a repo_lock_hooks line when repo locks are on and the working directory's repository declares a lock. The line says ok when the checkout runs the hook, and is a note saying hooks off when it does not. A session that starts in that checkout sees the same thing at the head of its briefing, as a LOCK hooks off line (see repo locks in the briefing).

It finds the hooks folder as git does. core.hooksPath is read from your global git config, the repository's config and, with extensions.worktreeConfig on, the worktree's config.worktree; the last one to set it wins. Otherwise the folder is the repository's own .git/hooks. The reference-transaction file there must be executable, with a line, not a comment, that runs seam lock check.

It does not follow the system git config, include and includeIf, a -c on one git command, or the config-defined hooks (hook.<name>.command) that newer gits also run. A checkout set up through one of those shows hooks off even when git runs the check.

What you see while it runs

The console is read-mostly and live over SSE - it is how you watch a fleet without being in its loop.

Screen What it answers
/console/tasks Ready, In progress, Blocked (with each task's blockers), Closed - the queue at a glance
A task's detail panel Who claims it, whether the lease is live or expired, and the release-lock button
/console/sessions Which agents are alive, and each one's claimed tasks with remaining lease
A project's detail The plan timeline - each step's status, holder, and lease
/console/plans Captured plans with status, iteration, and task progress

The same view without a browser:

seam ready --blocked                 # the queue plus what is blocking what
seam task list --status in_progress  # what is claimed right now
seam sessions --status active        # who is alive

A task that reads claim lapsed - in progress, its lease run out - is the signature of a crashed holder. If the gardener is running, leave it - the reaper will return it. If you need it now, release the claim.

One more collision to know about

Coordination has a scope failure mode, not just a queue one. When several agents are live in different repos and one of them writes durable knowledge without a bound session, Seamless cannot tell which project the write belongs to - and refuses it as ambiguous rather than inheriting from whichever ambient session was most recent. That refusal is the feature: the alternative is one agent's memory silently landing in another agent's project.

Claude Code and Codex agents are bound to their own sessions automatically, so this bites hookless clients and agents on an older seam. Bind the session (Integrate your agent), or pass project explicitly. See Projects & scope.
